introduction-deploy-release.core: Deploying puts code on servers; releasing exposes it to users. Separating the two (with flags and gradual traffic shifting) lets you ship code continuously and release features deliberately and gradually.

first_principles.problem: When deploying and releasing are the same event, every deploy is a high-stakes moment for all users.
truths: Code can run in production while staying invisible.
Exposure can be controlled per user or percentage.
Gradual exposure limits the blast radius.

analogy.title: A chef cooking a new dish before adding it to the menu
analogy.story: It's prepared in the kitchen, served to a few regulars first, and only then printed on the menu.
analogy.breaks: Dark code still runs some paths and needs testing, and flags add complexity.

example.title: Launching a redesign
example.outcome: releases become business decisions, not deploy events.

check.q: What's the difference between deploy and release?
check.a: Deploying installs code in production; releasing makes it visible to users.

feature-flags-the-fundamental-switch.core: A feature flag wraps a code path in a runtime-evaluated condition (on/off, percentage, user segment), controlled from a flag service, so features can be turned on, targeted or killed without a deploy.

first_principles.problem: Turning off a broken feature normally requires an emergency rollback deploy.
truths: Conditions can be changed at runtime.
derivation: **if flags.enabled('x', user)** around the new path.
Use a **kill switch** for instant disable.

analogy.title: A light switch wired to a lamp in another room
analogy.story: The wiring (deploy) is done; the switch (flag) decides when the light goes on.
analogy.breaks: Flag evaluation must be fast and resilient, so cache it and have defaults if the flag service is down.

steps.label: Kill
steps.detail: Errors spike, so set the flag to 0%: instant, no deploy.

check.q: What should happen if the flag service is unreachable?
check.a: The SDK falls back to a safe default value (usually off).

canary-deployments-testing-with-real-tra.core: A canary routes a small percentage of real traffic to the new version and compares its health against the stable version before widening exposure, catching problems that only real traffic reveals.

first_principles.problem: Staging can't reproduce real traffic patterns, data and scale.
truths: Production traffic is the only true test.

analogy.title: The canary in the coal mine
analogy.story: A small early-warning signal protects everyone else.
analogy.breaks: At low traffic you need longer bake times to reach statistical confidence.

example.title: A canary of v2
example.outcome: problems are caught early with few users affected.

check.q: Why can't staging replace a canary?
check.a: Staging lacks real production traffic patterns, data and scale.

automated-canary-analysis-aca-removing-t.core: Automated canary analysis runs baseline and canary side by side, statistically compares their metrics (for example with Kayenta's Mann-Whitney test), scores the result, and promotes or rolls back automatically.

first_principles.problem: Humans watching dashboards are slow, inconsistent, biased toward shipping and asleep at 3 AM.
truths: Consistent criteria beat judgement under pressure.
derivation: Deploy a fresh **baseline** alongside the **canary** (same size and age).

analogy.title: A drug trial with a control group
analogy.story: Comparing treated patients to a matched control group shows the drug's real effect.
analogy.breaks: Bad metric choice gives confident wrong decisions, so pick SLI-aligned metrics.

example.title: Why a fresh baseline?
flow: Old prod pods: warm caches, long uptime

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Comparing against warm production is unfair to the canary.

check.q: Why deploy a new baseline instead of comparing to existing production?
check.a: So both groups have the same age and warm-up conditions, making the comparison fair.

putting-it-together-the-progressive-deli.core: A mature pipeline layers the techniques: merge, deploy dark behind a flag, canary with automated analysis, full deploy, then gradual flag rollout by segment, with automated rollback at every stage.

first_principles.problem: Flags and canaries used separately leave gaps: canaries catch infrastructure bugs, while flags control feature exposure.
truths: Infrastructure risk and feature risk are distinct.
Each stage needs its own exit criteria.

analogy.title: A double safety lock
analogy.story: One lock secures the building (canary deploy); the other secures each room (feature flags).
analogy.breaks: The more layers you add, the more operational complexity you take on.

example.title: Shipping a new recommendation engine
flow: Deploy with flag off via canary (ACA passes)

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Infrastructure and business risks are both controlled.

example.outcome: safe, measured delivery from code to everyone.

check.q: What does a canary catch that a feature flag rollout might not?
check.a: Deployment-level problems such as crashes, memory leaks or latency regressions in the new build.
